newsitem.title: MALDIVES: India, Pakistan see progress before Kashmir accord.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan see progress before Kashmir accord.

text.p: India and Pakistan said on Sunday that they expect to reach a series of agreements to ease longstanding tensions before resolving a 50-year quarrel over Kashmir.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan said a settlement over Kashmir would take "a long time", but progress in other areas such as relaxing travel restrictions, boosting bilateral trade and releasing prisoners could be expected sooner.

"Once we form groups to tackle the issues, then we'll see how it is, because Kashmir naturally will take a long time," Khan told reporters ahead of a summit meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in the Maldives.

"The other issues won't take so much time, and probably most of them would start showing results sooner than the Kashmir one," he said, adding that the two countries planned to set up groups to tackle each issue including Kashmir.
Khan's remarks indicated that while Pakistan continued to insist that Kashmir should figure on the agenda in bilateral talks, it was willing to allow progress in less contentious areas.

India welcomed Khan's remarks, which he made on the eve of face-to-face talks between his prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, and his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, in this Indian Ocean island state.

"That makes sense to us because that is what we have been saying, that intractable issues cannot be settled overnight," Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman Talmiz Ahmad told Reuters Television, citing Kashmir.
"There are very hard, national positions that have been taken, and it is not possible that you can have a resolution that would satisfy both sides.
"I think we must move forward on the other issues that can be resolved, and I think that some of the issues that have been mentioned are ones we can make progress on."

Both India and Pakistan continued to play down expectations of any major progress at the Monday's planned talks between Gujral and Sharif, the first meeting between the nations' prime ministers in more than four years.
The two countries launched fresh peace talks in March, when their foreign secretaries -- highest ranking civil servants in the foreign ministries -- met in Delhi.
Khan said Islamabad and Delhi had hoped that the foreign secretaries could hold a second round before the prime ministers met, but it never took place.
"We should not build up hopes because the groundwork has not been done, the agenda has not been drawn. In any case, it is positive that they (Sharif and Gujral) are meeting," he said.
Asked to describe Monday's meeting between Gujral and Sharif, Khan said: "It would be ice-breaking, it would give a direction to the foreign secretaries' meeting that would take place in Islamabad."
The Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman called Monday's meeting informal and said he did not expect any major announcements although the dates of talks between foreign secretaries could be announced.

"This is a getting-to-know meeting. There is no specific agenda before them. It is a means of getting together," Ahmad said. "It is an extremely important occasion, but I don't think any detailed discussions would take place within the constraints of the time."
